issue_context.title: kubelet DRA plugin not cleaning resources if kubelet restarted
issue_context.body:
### What happened?

The dynamic resource created by kubelet DRA plugin is not cleaned because NodeUnprepareResource  is not called. 

### What did you expect to happen?

kubelet  DRA plugin will free the allocated dynamic resource

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. create a POD with Dynamic Resources
2. restart kubelet
3. delete Pod 

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

review_comments: I don't see this comment anymore. I understand that generateCDIAnnotations call was moved to another file, but the comment was either forgotten or dropped on purpose. Can you elaborate?
mmm, I forgot it in the rebase. I will fix it in the next PR spin.
nit: capitalize the comment
I think it capitalize  to refer the annotations field below. Are you sure you want this change?
ah right, in this case lower-case makes sense
nit: let's move this above the annotation generation so that they are created in the same order they get added to the `ClaimInfo` struct.

If we did as suggested above, then it would be here that I would imagine we take the state we just pulled, and we update the cache with both it, and any derived information before building the manager below.
@moshe010 can you explain why this check was removed?
This was at my request. Calling `add()` should be an idempotent operation that never fails. I would be OK with a warning here if you prefer, but it feels wrong to have it error out.
I'm a bit concerned that we can silently rewrite already cached information this way. I'd prefer to at least issue a warning.
In C++ I would put an assert here because if we ever hit this there is a bug. So maybe using a Fatal log is appropriate?

conceptually panic in golang is an assert without condition, but I'm not sure we should panic here. this code is called when we prepare resources and that operation is indempotent, i.e. we might have the same or at least functionally the same result.
But it should never reach the  `add()` call because it is protected earlier by the call to `get()`.
In fact if it ever did reach the `add()` call a second time, it would error out because of the check that was previously there ...
So do we agree that adding  log a warning is sufficient?

> But it should never reach the add() call because it is protected earlier by the call to get()

True, but it's done on the caller side, so can be changed there. Checking that we're not rewriting data still makes sense to me.

I guess it comes down to how you view the API. To me, I think of `delete()`, `get()` and `add()` as all being idempotent and should explicitly not do any checking. They should blindly do what is told of them (and if you wanted to do any checking, this should happen outside of these calls -- which is in fact what we are currently doing).

My understanding was that `add` should add, but not rewrite. That was a reason to check it. You're right, it was an assertion, something not expected, but potentially dangerous and therefore worth checking.

If we keep the check, then I would argue we also need to introduce a check on `delete()` through the same reasoning. Though I would still argue it is not necessary from my point of view in either call.
I'm ok with this. Just thought it would be harder to debug silent cache rewrites. As for `delete` call - it's harmless to attempt deleting something that was already deleted.

Something that came out of reviewing:

To future proof this, let's store it as a map, where the key is the name of the kubelet plugin. For now there will only be one entry (whose name is the same as the `DriverName`), but in the future there will be multiple entries.

Actually. I will fold this into my changes for https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/116332 which is where it becomes relevant anyway. If for some reason it becomes clear that that PR wont make it, we can pull it out as a standalone change so we don't have to change the checkpointing format in 1.28.
Would it make sense to rename it to CDIDevices as we did for CRI?
Yes, but I will do this in a follow-up.
@moshe010 This looks like we're always verifying checksum 0. Am I missing something?
yes we don't want that the checksum will effect the output checksum  see https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/cm/memorymanager/state/checkpoint.go#L46-L51
@moshe010 I understand why marshalling code does that. My question is about verifying code. What's the point of verifying 0 checksum only?

we don't verify  0 checksum. we verify all the DRAManagerCheckpoint struct ( I am passing dc)   but before doing that we put checksum =0 because the struct include the checksum.  This is how we generated the checksum in the marshalling code so when we verify we passing the DRAManagerCheckpoint  struct with checksum =0.
ah, ok. now I understand. Thanks for the explanations!

We don't checkpoint annotations, but `Manager.GetResources` relies on them. This can cause empty annotations passed to the CRI runtime if Kubelet restarts between successful `PrepareResources` and `GetResources` calls.
I'd propose to get rid of this field and generate annotations on the fly.
but we regenerate them when kubelet restart in the newClaimInfoCache by calling newClaimInfo

I don't quite follow. We always generate the annotations anytime a claiminfo is created (in `newClaimInfo()`) -- whether that be directly after a (successful) `PrepareResources()` call or after a kubelet restart when repopulating the cache from the checkpoint.
It seems that annotations are re-generated when Kubelet restarts. Looks quite implicit to me.
So, we have 2 parts of cache. One part is checkpointed and another is generated, correct?
yes

We have a single cache that contains ClaimInfo objects. ClaimInfo objects contain (1) state that is checkpointed and (2) meta information that can be generated from that checkpointed state (for convenience). Right now this meta information is just the annotations but could be other things later on.

Anytime a new claimInfo object is created it fills all of its fields (both those that will eventually be checkpointed AND the generated information).

So from the perspective of someone using the cache, all they need to know is that it contains ClaimInfo objects and that these objects are always fully populated with the data they store.
And we have to remember to re-generate meta information when we restore state, correct?
It's not about remembering -- its all encapsulated in the body of the `newClaimInfo()` call. Just as with any `new*()` call you do what's necessary to populate your fields.
Now it started to make sense to me. Thanks for the explanations!
No worries. Thanks for probing. Keeps us honest.

It feels strange to me to hang all of these functions off of the state type. I would expect the state type to do exactly one thing -- act as the state store for any checkpointed information. The cache should then be a type in this package that may or may not extend the state type directly, that can then add this additional functionality if desired.

We should consider checkpointing here and in the similar places.
Actually, if we decide to checkpoint on every change we may want to return back to checkpointing in the claimInfo methods (`add`, `delete`, `addPodReference` etc).

I think the motivation for also checkout after NodePrepareResource to avoid calling the grpc again if we didn't checkpoint it at the end of the PrepareResources.  for example one DRA plugin succeed (checkpoint it) second DRA plugin failed. 

And the reason for UnNodePrepareResource is to be similar to PrepareResources flow. 

now I am rethinking that anyway we can't cover all the corner cases see [1] with this logic so maybe we will do checkpoint at just the end of the PrepareResources/UnPrepareResources  for this phase. 

[1] - 
the corner case we try to provide solution was:
1. Pod created
2. Pod passed to kubelet
3. PrepareResources call is made in the kubelet
4. Some number of underlying gRPC calls to plugins’ PrepareResources succeeds
5. kubelet is taken offline before checkpoint happens
6. PrepareResources call to the kubelet times out
7. Pod enters failed state because it was never able to be started on the node
8. Pod gets deleted
9. Plugins have state about a now deleted pod without the ability to ever recover from that

I don't like the idea of the checkpointing being implicit in the various `add()` and `delete()` calls.

It would be fine to move this call up and call it more frequently, but I feel strongly about not embedding it in the calls.
I'm ok with both ways of doing it. In fact we seem to do it on any cache change anyway.
Why we should convert `claimInfo` map to the list?

because we don't want to relay on the calimInfo cache key. Currently it claimName+namespace in the future it can be something else. if we checkpoint it and change it in the future we will need to migrate from old format to new format of the key.

This could, in theory, be done under the hood, but in any case, I don't think we should checkpoint the whole map (i.e. including the key that is made up of the claimName+claimNamespace). It made more since in this case to then do the translation to a list at this level so that the underling `state` type only ever operates on a list and not a map.

This method assumes that we have enough info in the checkpoint to reconstruct the cache from it. In this particular case it means that we must always have a claim name and a namespace in the checkpoint data. This assumption is a bit concerning.

@moshe010
> Currently it claimName+namespace in the future it can be something else.

true. However, in this case you'll have to add this something else to the checkpoint data, which would be a format change anyway. Otherwise you won't be able to restore the cache from the checkpoint.

The other way to look at it is that we are simply checkpointing the full state of the claim necessary to:
1. make future `NodeUnprepareResource()` calls on already prepared resources
2. cache any information necessary for exposure through the PodResources API

This is exactly what we store in the checkpoint -- no more, no less. What do you find concerning about this?

> What do you find concerning about this?

The fact that we store only part of the cache and changing its structure. I find it a bit concerning, but don't feel strongly about it.

I don't share your concern. Only the bits absolutely necessary for checkpointing are synced to disk and everything else that can be generated from that (for convenience) is done so as the cache is repopulated after a kubelet restart.
What's the purpose of this division?
Less churn in the checkpoint format (since it only stores the essentials) and the ability to easily add meta-fields as we see fit hanging off of the claimInfo struct.

I'm generally ok with this. It's more complex than storing the whole cache though. I'm not sure it makes much sense currently as we only generate annotations, but it can make sense in future if we have more metadata, especially if that metadata is hard or time consuming to generate.
